query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lightweight high‐entropy alloys that achieve a homogeneous, highly disordered (amorphous or nanocrystalline solid solution) microstructure with pronounced lattice distortion establish continuous, protective oxide films under high‐temperature and corrosive conditions; this uniform microstructure simultaneously enhances mechanical strength and corrosion/oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight HEA (e.g. an Al–Ti–V–Nb based film) synthesized by magnetron sputtering that exhibits an amorphous or uniformly nanocrystalline structure with minimal secondary phase segregation.
generation.intervention: Processing modification (e.g., controlled sputtering/heat treatment) that reinforces microstructural homogeneity and optimizes lattice distortion, compared to a similar HEA prepared with less controlled conditions leading to heterogeneous or partially crystallized microstructures.
generation.conditions: Under high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 800–1000 °C) and exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution), where a uniform, continuous protective oxide layer is necessary to maintain performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform amorphous or nanocrystalline solid solution that minimizes local compositional fluctuations and defect concentrations, thereby promoting a continuous, self-healing oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced lattice distortion and chemical disorder in the homogeneous microstructure impede dislocation motion and crack initiation, while concurrently facilitating the rapid formation of a protective oxide film. This film lowers oxygen and corrosive ion diffusivity, ensuring both mechanical integrity and surface passivation during extreme environmental exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy with a less uniform, heterogeneous microstructure (which might contain coarse intermetallics or phase separations), the processed alloy will show higher compressive strength, lower corrosion current density, and a reduced oxidation mass gain over time.
generation.baseline: A comparable lightweight HEA manufactured without the microstructural refinement treatment that results in heterogeneous phase distribution and less effective oxide film formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds under conditions where the protective oxide remains stable; if the operating temperature or corrosive severity exceeds the stability limits of the passivating oxide, the benefit of the homogeneous microstructure will diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in mechanical strength and corrosion/oxidation resistance is composition‐ and processing‐dependent, and quantifying the relative contributions of lattice distortion versus oxide film formation requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of lightweight HEA films with similar chemical compositions: one group processed under conditions designed to produce a homogeneous amorphous/nanocrystalline microstructure, and a control group processed under conditions that promote microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., partial crystallization with secondary phase precipitates). Expose both groups to identical high-temperature oxidation (e.g., isothermal TGA at 900 °C for 200 hours) and corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution) while measuring mechanical strength via nano-compression tests.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/XRD) to verify homogeneity vs heterogeneity
Corrosion current densities (Icorr) and open circuit potentials (Ecorr)
Oxidation kinetics via mass gain over time (TGA data)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogeneous HEA films do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., lower Icorr, reduced oxidation mass gain, and higher compressive strength) compared to heterogeneous films under the same test conditions, then the hypothesis that microstructural homogeneity mediates the simultaneous enhancement of mechanical, corrosion, and oxidation resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: However, the strong HEA films mentioned above suffer from low ductility in general. How to balance the strength and ductility of amorphous HEA films is important for their applications in the field of flexible microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials. In addition, seeking a high-performance HEA film with low density and corrosion resistance is of great significance for their applications in extreme conditions. In these cases, it is crucial to develop a high hardness, high strength–ductility synergy, and excellent corrosion resistance of amorphous lightweight high entropy alloy film. In this work, the lightweight AlTiVNb HEA film was prepared by magnetron sputtering, and the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance were investigated.

High-specific-strength materials play a critical role in engineering applications, especially for the aerospace and automobile industries, as they can reduce the weight of structural parts and achieve energy conservation [,]. The RHEAs reported in previous studies usually have a higher density and lower specific strength [,,], which restrict their engineering applications. Thus, the development of RHEAs with high specific strength has become a critical issue. The unique elemental composition of RHEAs provides extensive freedom when designing alloys with desired performances and tuning properties [,,]. Senkov et al. [,] selected refractory elements with low density including Ti, V, Cr, Zr and Nb, and developed the CrNbTiVZr alloy system. The density of the CrNbTiVZr alloy system ranges from 6.34 g/cm3 to 6.67 g/cm3, and the CrNbTiVZr RHEA has a maximum specific strength approaching 200 MPa·cm3·g−1. Although the CrNbTiVZr alloy system has a low density, the specific strength still needs to be further improved. Benefiting from the abundant elemental composition of RHEAs, adjusting the type and content of elements has been widely used in the development of high-specific-strength RHEAs.
